title: Guru Amar Das close
hookLine: humility, equality, and a kitchen open to all

cards: Steam rising off big pots. Someone stirring dal with a paddle as long as an arm. Rows of people on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and a volunteer coming down the line with a bucket of rotis, one into each open palm.
A farmer, a banker, a stranger who wandered in: same floor, same food, same hands serving it.
That kitchen is where our time with Guru Amar Das ends, because the hymns of the past days show up in it, cooked down to something you can eat.

teach.b: Three threads run through his time, and the kitchen ties them together. Humility. Tradition remembers him as a servant long before anyone called him Guru, carrying water in the dark.
His hymns warn about haumai, ego, and say ego and the Name can't share one room. In the langar, nobody eats in a place of honor. Equality.

teach.h: EQUALITY: THE WELL, THE MANJIS, THE PYRE.
teach.b: Tradition remembers his well at Goindval as open to every caste, his teachers on their manjis as women and men, and his voice against a tax on pilgrims. He took the word sati off the pyre and gave it to faithful lives.
In the langar, nobody asks who your family is before the roti is handed over. And a kitchen open to all.
Sikh tradition gives Guru Amar Das a large part in making the langar central, so that those who came to see the Guru sat in the row and ate first. The meal became a teaching about who belongs.

teach.h: THE HYMNS IN THE CLATTER OF POTS.
teach.b: You can hear the old Guru's voice in the clatter of the pots. O mind, you are the form of light, and so, in the Sikh view, is the person beside you. The world is burning, so feed whoever comes, by any door.
Face the Guru, not only yourself. Let ego die a little in the serving. And when the mind is restless, rest in the Word, then pick up the bucket and walk the row.
Tomorrow, his successor, Guru Ram Das, and the shape of a Sikh's morning.

how: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and serve and everyone sits together on the floor or at shared tables; Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's part in it, along with his hymns, on his gurpurab.

games.q: what does “guru amar das close” mean?
o: the closing of the gurdwara he founded at Goindval
humility, equality and a kitchen open to all
the last hymn Guru Amar Das wrote before he died

games.q: Guru Amar Das, closed: tap the pairs.
p: the water carrier, warning against ego
a well and a row open to all
everyone eats in the same row

s: in the langar, important guests eat in a separate place of honor
everyone sits in the same row on the same floor, whoever they are.
Sikh tradition gives Guru Amar Das a large part in making the langar central
those who came to see the Guru sat in the row and ate first.

games.q: a hungry stranger from a caste others avoid walks into the Guru's kitchen. what happens?
o: they're seated in the same row and handed the same roti.
games.why: in the langar no one is asked who they are before the food is handed over. the same floor, the same food, for everyone.

practice: Picture your own kitchen, your table, or just your free hour this week, and the door to it: who usually comes through, and who never does?
Let one person come to mind who could use a seat, a neighbor, a new coworker, someone alone, and see them sitting down as something simple is handed to them. No grand plan, just the door opening.

wordCard.voice: Guru Amar Das close. Humility, equality and a kitchen open to all: the old Guru's hymns of ego, light and the Word, cooked down into a shared meal. Today's word.

orig.note: the Guru's free kitchen, where everyone sits in one row and eats the same meal.

carryVoice: Your line: open kitchen. Nobody is tested at the door before the roti comes. Same time tomorrow.
